title: Cache Invalidation
description: Removing or updating stale entries in a cache so callers never read outdated data after the underlying source changes.
contexts: Amazon showing a $29.99 price seconds after a seller drops it to $24.99
Cloudflare edge nodes still serving an old homepage after a marketing team deploys a site update
Shopify displaying items as in-stock after warehouse inventory hits zero
GitHub serving a stale README to visitors after a developer pushes new documentation
Slack showing a deactivated user as a valid recipient after an admin removes their account
YouTube caching a video thumbnail that the creator already replaced with a new one
Stripe dashboard listing a charge as pending after it has already been refunded

cards.headline: The update went live. Nobody can see it.
cards.body: The marketing team just pushed a new homepage, but users in Tokyo, Frankfurt, and Dallas are still seeing the old one. A [[CDN|network of servers that caches content near users]] like Cloudflare has hundreds of [[edge nodes|CDN servers placed close to users, around the globe]] holding [[stale|outdated cached entries that no longer match the current source]] copies of the old page. There are exactly two ways to fix this: wait for those copies to expire on their own, or reach in and delete them right now.

cards.headline: Two ways to fix a stale cache

left.label: TTL Expiry
points: Cached copy auto-expires after a set time
Stale window lasts up to the full TTL after a change
Marketing waits an hour to see their update

right.label: Purge on Deploy
points: Deploy pipeline calls the CDN purge API
Edge copies deleted the moment you push
Requires wiring in the deploy pipeline
Marketing sees the update go live in seconds

cards.headline: Pick a number and live with it
cards.body: With a [[TTL|how long a cached copy stays valid before it expires automatically]], you make one upfront bet. Set it to one hour and a broken layout or outdated headline can sit in cache for 60 minutes after you push a fix. Set it to 5 seconds and the CDN barely helps, because most requests hit the [[origin server|the main server holding the current, live version of content]] directly instead of the cached copy.

cards.headline: Purging skips the countdown
cards.body: When the deploy pipeline finishes, it calls Cloudflare's API to [[purge|explicitly delete one or more cached entries from the CDN right now]] the old homepage across every edge node. Every copy is marked invalid within seconds, and the next visitor triggers a fresh fetch from the origin. No TTL countdown required.

cards.headline: Purge on deploy, step by step

steps.label: Developer pushes to main
steps.detail: New homepage code lands in version control

steps.label: CI/CD pipeline runs
steps.detail: [[CI/CD pipeline|automated system that builds and deploys code on each push]] puts new files on the origin server

steps.label: Pipeline calls the CDN purge API
steps.detail: Sends the homepage URL as the target to invalidate

steps.label: CDN marks all edge copies invalid
Next visitor hits an edge node
steps.detail: Edge node has no valid cached copy: cache miss

steps.label: Edge node fetches from origin
steps.detail: New homepage stored in cache and returned to visitor

cards.question: The marketing team deployed a homepage update at noon. The CDN has a 1-hour TTL and no purge call was made. What are visitors seeing at 12:45 PM?
options: The old homepage, because the TTL has not expired yet
The new homepage, because CDNs detect file changes automatically
A mix of old and new, because edge nodes update at different rates
cards.explanation: A TTL is a simple countdown timer. It has no awareness that the origin changed. Until that hour ticks to zero, every edge node serves the cached copy it has, and visitors get the old page.
optionExplanations: CDNs do not poll the origin for changes. They serve a cached copy until its TTL expires or a purge call arrives. Automatic change detection would require constant polling and would defeat the purpose of caching.

Without a purge signal, there is no propagation event to create a mix. All edge nodes hold the same stale copy and expire at the same wall-clock time, so the transition to fresh content happens uniformly when the TTL runs out.

cards.headline: A cache purge on the wire

cards.body: Keeping a cache fresh is just a TTL tuning problem. Set a short enough TTL and your cache never serves stale data.

cards.headline: TTL is a fallback, not a solution
cards.body: A TTL gives staleness a hard deadline, but it does nothing the moment the source changes. Between a deploy at noon and a TTL expiry at 1 PM, every edge node worldwide faithfully serves yesterday's page. [[Cache invalidation|removing or updating stale cached entries so every caller gets current data]] means acting at the moment of change, not waiting out a countdown.

cards.headline: The scale of the problem
cards.context: A targeted cache purge propagates to all of them in a few seconds. Relying on TTL expiry alone for the same result could mean waiting an hour or more, depending on what you set.

cards.question: Site A caches its homepage with a 1-hour TTL and no purge wiring. Site B fires a CDN purge call at the end of every deploy. Both deploy a new homepage at noon. Which site is still showing the old homepage to visitors at 12:55 PM, and why?
options: Site A, because its cached copies stay marked valid until the TTL ticks to zero at 1 PM
Site B, because propagating a purge to hundreds of edge nodes takes several minutes
cards.explanation: Site A's edge nodes hold a copy they believe is valid until 1 PM. They have no signal that anything changed at the origin, so visitors for the next 65 minutes get the old page. Site B's purge completed in seconds, so its visitors saw the new page almost immediately after the deploy.
optionExplanations: Purge propagation across a large CDN completes in a few seconds, not minutes. CDNs are specifically built to distribute invalidation signals fast. The misconception is that scale slows purge down to something comparable to TTL expiry, but those two timescales are not even close.

cards.body: Cache invalidation is one of the two problems Phil Karlton famously called the hardest in computer science. Every time a site redesign goes live and looks right everywhere within seconds, a purge call ran behind the scenes. The TTL countdown that was supposed to handle it would still have 55 minutes left.
